main_damage_causes: Systematic removal of Dumbledore's whimsical, eccentric personality markers (nonsense speech, school song, lemon drops, socks exchange, earmuffs quip) that collectively define his distinctive voice and distinguish him from a generic wise mentor

Compression of key dialogue scenes (Privet Drive, hospital wing) that establish the texture of Dumbledore's relationship with Harry — partial truths delivered with warmth, philosophical depth, and deliberate evasiveness — reducing him to a functional plot-explainer

Loss of small but cumulative physical and tonal details (sitting on the floor with Harry, solitary farewell at the corner, twinkling eyes at the twins) that signal Dumbledore's emotional investment and omniscient-yet-indulgent awareness, flattening a layered portrait into dignified authority

Collapse of the private, morally weighty reckoning between Dumbledore and Harry (book scenes after the flying car) into procedural efficiency, losing the characterisation of Dumbledore's disappointment as his most powerful tool

Replacement of Dumbledore's Socratic pedagogical method — guiding Harry to conclusions through patient questioning — with more direct statement of lessons, flattening a defining aspect of his mentorship voice

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 1 — Dumbledore arrives on Privet Drive and greets McGonagall
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book establishes Dumbledore as whimsical, unhurried, and gently humorous: he chuckles at the cat, mutters 'I should have known,' offers lemon drops, jokes about blushing since Madam Pomfrey complimented his earmuffs, and engages McGonagall with warm, teasing wit. The exchange is rich with personality — playful deflection, quiet authority, and genuine warmth.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film compresses the entire Privet Drive conversation to a handful of functional lines. All lemon-drop comedy, the Voldemort-name lecture, the blushing/earmuffs quip, and the extended back-and-forth with McGonagall are cut. Dumbledore's opening line shifts from the book's amused 'I should have known' (said to the cat) to the film's more formal 'I should've known that you would be here, Professor McGonagall' addressed directly to her after she transforms. The playful, eccentric register is largely absent.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The Privet Drive scene is the reader's first extended encounter with Dumbledore's character. The book uses it to establish his defining traits — eccentricity, warmth, dry humour, and moral gravity held in deliberate tension. The film reduces him to a functional plot-delivery figure, losing the personality foundation that makes later scenes (Mirror of Erised, hospital wing) land with full weight.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 1 — Dumbledore instructs Hagrid to leave, offers no farewell to Harry
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book has Dumbledore stand with McGonagall and Hagrid for a full minute looking at the baby, after which he says 'that's that' and suggests they join the celebrations. He personally lays Harry on the doorstep, tucks the letter in the blankets, then from the corner clicks the Put-Outer back on and murmurs 'Good luck, Harry' — a private, tender moment of farewell that reveals deep feeling beneath the composed exterior.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Dumbledore places Harry on the step and delivers 'Good luck, Harry Potter' as a group farewell while McGonagall and Hagrid are still present. The solitary, lingering moment Dumbledore has alone with the child at the corner — clicking the lights back on, watching from a distance — is cut entirely. Hagrid is dismissed with 'There, there, Hagrid. It's not really goodbye, after all,' which has no book equivalent and slightly diminishes the gravity.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book's closing image — Dumbledore alone at the corner, watching the bundle on the step, the twinkling light gone from his eyes — is one of the few moments where his private emotional life is briefly visible. Its removal flattens his relationship with Harry's fate from something personally felt to something administratively managed.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 1 — Dumbledore's justification for leaving Harry with the Dursleys
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Dumbledore gives a full reasoned defence: the Dursleys are Harry's only family; he will be famous before he can walk; it would be enough to turn any boy's head; growing up away from it all until he is ready is the wisest course. He looks 'very seriously' over his half-moon glasses and persuades a sceptical McGonagall through logic and care.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Dumbledore's justification is condensed to 'The only family he has' and 'He's better off growing up away from all of that. Until he is ready.' The deliberate reasoning about fame corrupting a child — the moral core of his decision — is largely cut, making the choice seem perfunctory rather than a carefully weighed judgment.
damaging_scenes.explanation: Dumbledore's willingness to place a child in a cold home is one of the saga's most morally complex decisions. The book shows it as a reasoned, reluctant choice grounded in long-term thinking. The film's compression makes it appear arbitrary, reducing audience understanding of a motivation that resonates across the entire series.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 6 — Dumbledore's start-of-term speech (Sorting ceremony)
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Dumbledore rises, beams at students with arms wide open, delivers the nonsense words ('Nitwit! Blubber! Oddment! Tweak!') as his entire welcome speech, then later leads the school song with evident delight — conducting the Weasley twins' funeral-march finale and clapping loudest of all, saying 'Ah, music. A magic beyond all we do here.' Percy's bemused reaction ('I think he might have told us prefects') underlines how Dumbledore's whimsy is real, not performative.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film cuts the 'Nitwit! Blubber! Oddment! Tweak!' speech entirely. Dumbledore's first words to the assembled school are the functional start-of-term notices (the Forest, the third-floor corridor). The school song and its joyful coda are absent. Dumbledore is presented as a dignified authority figure rather than a delightfully unpredictable one.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The nonsense speech and school song are the book's primary demonstration that Dumbledore operates by his own rules, that his eccentricity is genuine and joyful, and that his relationship with the students is warm rather than merely authoritative. Cutting both removes a defining characterisation beat that makes him feel like the singular figure Hagrid and others describe him as.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 7 — Dumbledore at the feast; interaction with Harry after Sorting
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book has Dumbledore give Harry a quiet, knowing acknowledgment after the Quidditch match ('Well done... nice to see you haven't been brooding about that mirror... been keeping busy... excellent...') and during the feast provides contextual warmth and gentle authority. His twinkling eyes flashing at the Weasley twins regarding the forest corridor show his awareness and indulgence of students.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: In the film feast scene (Scene 7), Dumbledore lifts his goblet and gives Harry a slight congratulatory wave after Sorting — a visual gesture replacing any dialogue. The twinkling-eyes detail directed at the Weasley twins during the corridor warning is absent; the warning itself is delivered as a straight announcement with no accompanying wit or awareness.
damaging_scenes.explanation: Minor but consistent flattening: the film removes small signals that Dumbledore sees everything and responds to it with amusement rather than mere authority. Each individual cut is small, but cumulatively they strip the portrait of its texture.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 10 — Mirror of Erised conversation
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Dumbledore sits on the floor beside Harry, equalising their positions. He explains the mirror at length, asks Harry to think rather than just telling him, then gives the socks answer to 'what do you see?' — and the narrator notes Harry suspected Dumbledore 'might not have been quite truthful.' He asks Harry not to go looking for it again and says 'It does not do to dwell on dreams and forget to live.' He also tells Harry the mirror will be moved and mentions that Ron saw himself as head boy, demonstrating omniscience with lightness.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film retains the core explanation and the 'dwell on dreams' line but cuts Dumbledore sitting on the floor with Harry (he merely walks up and stands), cuts the socks exchange entirely, and cuts the Ron/head-boy observation. The exchange is shorter and more didactic, losing the playful depth (socks as possible deflection) and the physical gesture of equality (sitting on the floor).
damaging_scenes.explanation: The socks exchange is the clearest single illustration of Dumbledore's layered self-concealment — humour as shield, wisdom delivered obliquely. Its removal, combined with the loss of the floor-sitting gesture, makes the scene a lecture rather than a meeting between two people, reducing the warmth and complexity of his relationship with Harry.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 12 — Hospital wing; Dumbledore explains the Stone and Quirrell
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Dumbledore gives a long, philosophically rich conversation: he explains love's protection at length, discusses Nicolas Flamel and death with 'to the well-organised mind, death is but the next great adventure,' answers Harry's questions about Snape's motives (debt to James Potter), explains the invisibility cloak provenance with a twinkle, and deflects with 'just the one?' when Harry has more questions. He is warm, evasive about Voldemort's return question ('not today... when you are ready'), and the entire scene establishes his relationship with Harry as one of guided, partial truth.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film retains the Stone explanation, love-as-protection, and the Flamel death exchange but cuts: the Snape/James debt explanation entirely; the cloak provenance (no mention of James leaving it); the philosophical framing of death; the 'Alas, the first thing you ask me I cannot tell you' evasion about Voldemort's original motive; and the 'just the one?' exchange. The Bertie Bott's vomit-bean gag is added (no book equivalent in this scene). The conversation is noticeably shorter and less philosophically weighted.
damaging_scenes.explanation: This scene is the primary site where Dumbledore's relationship with Harry is established as one of careful, loving partial disclosure — telling Harry some truths, withholding others with stated reasons, and doing so with warmth and humour. Cutting the Snape explanation also removes a key piece of Snape's arc. The loss of the cloak provenance severs a James Potter connection. Together these cuts meaningfully reduce Dumbledore's relational and narrative function in the adaptation.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 13 — End-of-year feast; House Cup ceremony
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Dumbledore's speech includes 'Yes, yes, well done, Slytherin' before pivoting to last-minute points, the 'there are all kinds of courage' framing for Neville's award, and a clapping of hands that transforms the decorations. He radiates theatrical delight in upending the expected outcome. His earlier Christmas dinner appearance (flowered bonnet, chuckling at Flitwick's joke) also adds festive eccentricity.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film retains the structure of the House Cup scene faithfully, including 'it takes a great deal of bravery to stand up to your enemies, but a great deal more to stand up to your friends' and the banner transformation. This scene is largely faithful. The Christmas dinner detail (flowered bonnet) is absent but that is a minor omission.
damaging_scenes.explanation: Minor: the Christmas bonnet detail is a small eccentric touch absent from the film. The House Cup scene itself is well-executed and causes minimal damage.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 2 (Snape's office) — Dumbledore's handling of Harry and Ron's punishment
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scene 17: Dumbledore gives Harry a long, penetrating silence before speaking, making Harry feel unable to meet his eyes due to the weight of his disappointment. Dumbledore asks Harry to explain himself and listens carefully, choosing not to press on the car's ownership. The interaction is quiet, weighty, and deeply characterised by Dumbledore's perceptive, patient authority. Book Scene 23: Dumbledore calmly deflects Snape's punitive impulse and sweeps him away with gracious authority, maintaining full control of the situation.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film Scene 2: Dumbledore's line 'I'm well aware of our bylaws, Severus, having written more than a few myself' and his quick deferral to McGonagall is efficient but removes the extended private reckoning between Dumbledore and Harry entirely. There is no moment of Harry being unable to meet Dumbledore's gaze, no disappointment, no careful probing. Dumbledore then closes with the light quip about the custard tart, moving straight from authority to levity. The book's scene of quiet, weighty moral authority is collapsed into procedural expediency.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book establishes a key Dumbledore trait: his disappointment is more crushing than anger, and he uses silence and penetrating observation as tools of moral authority. The film removes the private reckoning and Harry's shame, replacing it with brisk procedure. The custard tart joke, present in both, lands differently without the preceding gravity — in the film it reads as immediate levity rather than a deliberate tonal release after serious engagement.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 3 (Dumbledore's office / Fawkes burning day)
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scenes 101–121: When Dumbledore enters after Fawkes burns, he smiles warmly and chuckles at Harry's stunned expression, engaging Harry with gentle warmth and explaining phoenixes with evident delight. He then seats himself and fixes Harry with his 'penetrating, light-blue stare,' preparing to probe him. The scene establishes Dumbledore's blend of warmth, wit, and deep attentiveness. Book Scene 121: Dumbledore firmly and immediately tells Hagrid he does not think Harry attacked anyone, showing decisive trust.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film Scene 3 (scene 77): The Fawkes exchange is reproduced closely and Dumbledore's warmth is present. However, the key divergence is in the subsequent private conversation: in the film Harry says 'No, Professor. Nothing' when asked if there is anything he'd like to share, and Dumbledore simply accepts this without the book's sense of Dumbledore already knowing there is something Harry is hiding and gently leaving the door open. The book's Dumbledore 'considered him, the tips of his long fingers together' in prolonged, searching silence before asking. The film collapses this into a brief exchange.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book's version of this scene carefully shows Dumbledore's almost supernatural perceptiveness — he knows Harry is withholding something about the voice and leaves space for Harry to come forward. The film accepts Harry's denial at face value, making Dumbledore slightly less omniscient and less invested in Harry's inner life. This is a recurring characterisation loss: Dumbledore's ability to see through people without pressing them is a defining trait.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 3 (scene 67) — Colin Creevey attack / Chamber confirmed open
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scenes 88–91: When McGonagall asks what it means, Dumbledore says 'The question is not who... the question is, how,' demonstrating his characteristic habit of thinking several steps ahead of everyone else and already focusing on the mechanism rather than the culprit. This is a precise illustration of his singular intellect.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film Scene 3 (scene 67): Dumbledore instead says 'It means our students are in great danger, Minerva... The Chamber of Secrets is indeed open again.' This is accurate information but loses the key line about 'not who, but how' — the moment that shows Dumbledore's mind operating at a different level from everyone else in the room.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book's 'The question is not who... the question is, how' is one of the clearest signals in CoS that Dumbledore already suspects the nature of the threat (a creature, not a student acting alone) and is thinking about mechanism rather than blame. Its removal flattens his intellectual distinctiveness in this scene to a straightforward confirmation of bad news.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 4 (scene 114) — Dumbledore's suspension / departure from Hagrid's hut
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scenes 146–168: Dumbledore explicitly and forcefully states 'I want it understood, Cornelius, that Hagrid has my full confidence' with eyes 'full of a fire Harry had never seen before.' When handed the suspension order, Dumbledore speaks his famous lines 'very slowly and clearly so that none of them could miss a word' — a deliberate, measured act of communication directed at Harry, who is hidden. The book emphasises this is a speech act of precision and trust, not resignation.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film Scene 4 (scene 114): The film reproduces the key speech ('I will only truly have left this school when none here are loyal to me... help will always be given at Hogwarts to those who ask for it') and adds the stage direction that Dumbledore's eyes 'drift — unmistakably — to Harry,' making the communication to Harry explicit. This is largely faithful and arguably enhances the moment visually. The 'fire in his eyes' when defending Hagrid is present as 'steely-eyed.' This scene is substantially faithful.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The film handles this scene well. The one minor loss is the book's emphasis on the 'fire' in Dumbledore's eyes specifically when defending Hagrid — a moment of rare visible emotion that characterises how deeply Dumbledore's loyalty runs. The film's 'steely-eyed' replaces passion with composure. Minor damage only.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 4 (scene 135) — Post-Chamber office scene, Dumbledore's conversation with Harry about Riddle/Voldemort
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scenes 233–250: Dumbledore opens by thanking Harry and noting that only real loyalty could have summoned Fawkes. He then listens carefully as Harry raises his worry about similarities with Riddle, responding with the 'It is our choices, Harry' speech delivered with great deliberateness. Crucially, Dumbledore also addresses the Sorting Hat question with gentle probing questions ('Think,' he says, waiting for Harry to arrive at the answer himself) and physically hands Harry the sword as proof. The scene is a sustained piece of mentorship.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film Scene 4 (scene 135): The film reproduces the key beats — the loyalty/Fawkes point, the Parseltongue explanation, the 'it's not our abilities but our choices' line (slightly reworded), and the sword. However, the film's Dumbledore delivers the key lesson more directly ('It's not our abilities that show what we truly are, Harry. It's our choices') without the book's Socratic method of asking Harry to think and arrive there himself. The book's 'Put you in Gryffindor. Listen to me, Harry... Think' becomes the film's more direct statement.
damaging_scenes.explanation: One of Dumbledore's most important pedagogical traits in the books is that he guides Harry to conclusions rather than stating them. The film's version of this climactic mentor scene delivers the lesson more directly, losing the Socratic texture. The core content is preserved, so damage is moderate, but the method — which is as important as the message for characterising Dumbledore — is somewhat flattened.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 4 (scene 135) — Dumbledore's confrontation with Lucius Malfoy on his return
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scenes 253–271: Dumbledore returns with serene confidence, immediately discomfiting Malfoy with calm precision. He methodically walks Malfoy through the implication of the diary — the political damage to the Weasleys, the threat to Muggle-borns — before landing the implied accusation: 'One would hope that no more of Lord Voldemort's old school things find their way into innocent hands.' The book Dumbledore is surgically precise, enjoying the exposure of Malfoy while maintaining perfect composure. He also allows Harry to give the diary back, trusting Harry's instincts without explanation.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film Scene 4 (scene 135): The film compresses this confrontation. Dumbledore mentions the governors' reversal and the implicit coercion ('several of them seemed under the impression that you would curse their families'), then delivers the warning about 'Lord Voldemort's old school things' with 'a chill to his voice.' The political dismantling of Malfoy's position (the Weasley/Muggle Protection Act angle) is cut. The film Dumbledore is still authoritative but less surgically devastating.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book's Dumbledore actively and deliberately exposes the full political implications of Malfoy's scheme, depriving him of any plausible deniability before landing the warning. This is Dumbledore functioning as a chess player, not just a headmaster. The film reduces this to a more straightforward warning, losing the demonstration of Dumbledore's strategic intelligence and his willingness to wield it against those who threaten his students.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 4 (scene 97) — Young Dumbledore / Riddle memory scene
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scenes 135–138: Young Dumbledore gives Riddle 'exactly the kind of penetrating stare Harry knew so well' — the book explicitly connects the 50-years-younger Dumbledore to the present Dumbledore via this characteristic look. He bids Riddle good night and strides off, but his watchfulness is clearly established. Book Scene 183: Riddle later says Dumbledore 'never seemed to like me as much as the other teachers did' and that he 'kept an annoyingly close watch on me.'
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film Scene 4 (scene 97): Young Dumbledore's exchange with Riddle is reproduced closely. He asks 'Is there something you wish to tell me, Tom?' — which is faithful. However, the film does not include the book's explicit narratorial note connecting young Dumbledore's penetrating stare to the present Dumbledore Harry knows. This is a minor loss of the continuity of character that the book deliberately establishes.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book uses the memory scene to show Harry recognising Dumbledore's characteristic gaze across fifty years, reinforcing that Dumbledore's perceptiveness is a deep and consistent part of who he is. The film's version is faithful in content but loses this explicit continuity signal. Minor damage.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 1 (Great Hall feast speech) - Dumbledore's opening remarks
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scene 12-17: Dumbledore opens with 'Welcome to another year at Hogwarts! I have a few things to say, and as one of them is very serious, I think it best to get it out of the way before you become befuddled by our excellent feast.' He leads with gravity, addresses the dementors first with clear solemnity, pausing to look 'very seriously around the hall' so that 'nobody moved or made a sound.'
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film Scene 1: Dumbledore opens with a jovial joke about 'flaming kiwi cups' being 'somewhat treacherous for those of us with facial hair,' requiring McGonagall to clear her throat to redirect him. The serious dementor announcement comes last rather than first, framed as an afterthought after the staff introductions.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book establishes that Dumbledore deliberately prioritises the serious warning before the feast, demonstrating his protective instincts and authoritative judgment. The film reorders this to make him appear bumbling and in need of correction by McGonagall, undermining his commanding gravitas and the trust Harry immediately feels in him. The book's Harry feels 'really calm for the first time since the dementor had entered the train compartment' specifically because of how Dumbledore carries himself; that effect is weakened when he opens with a joke that requires a colleague to steer him back on track.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 1 (Great Hall feast speech) - Dementor warning tone and content
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scenes 13-16: Dumbledore warns the students with explicit authority and controlled disapproval: 'I must make it plain that nobody is to leave school without permission... I therefore warn each and every one of you to give them no reason to harm you.' Book Scene 14 notes Harry remembers Dumbledore 'not being happy' about the dementors, conveying his restrained but clear resistance to their presence. Book Scene 79: Dumbledore states coldly, 'no dementor will cross the threshold of this castle while I am headmaster.'
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film Scene 1: The film omits Dumbledore's personal displeasure with the dementors entirely from the speech. He presents their presence as a straightforward Ministry arrangement ('at the request of the Ministry of Magic') without any of the book's undercurrent of reluctance or protective defiance. The cold declaration that no dementor will enter the castle while he is headmaster is absent from the feast scene.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book establishes Dumbledore as a figure who complies with Ministry requirements while making his own protective limits crystal clear. His personal displeasure with the dementors is a character beat that shows his moral compass operating independently of political pressure. The film's version makes him appear a neutral administrator passing on Ministry instructions, losing the dimension of principled resistance that defines him throughout this book.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 4 (Fat Lady portrait / Great Hall sleepover) - Dumbledore's command of the crisis
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scenes 40-55: Dumbledore arrives sweeping through the crowd, immediately issues precise orders to McGonagall and Filch, calmly interrogates Peeves (who 'didn't dare taunt Dumbledore'), and with one casual wave of his wand rearranges the entire Great Hall into a dormitory. He manages the castle search through the night, speaks with Snape at 3 a.m. with quiet authority, and shuts down Snape's insinuation about Lupin with a tone that makes 'it so clear that the subject was closed that Snape didn't reply.'
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film Scene 3-5: Dumbledore's instructions are compressed. He tells Filch to 'round up the ghosts' (a change from the book's McGonagall/Filch division of labour), and the overnight search scene is condensed. The film does retain his dismissal of Snape's insinuation about Lupin, but the extended demonstration of Dumbledore as the calm, methodical, magically powerful centre of the crisis response is significantly compressed, including the wand-wave that furnishes the hall.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book uses the Fat Lady crisis as a showcase for exactly why everyone trusts Dumbledore: he is unhurried, authoritative, magically capable, and politically clear-sighted under pressure. The film's compression reduces him to a few lines of instruction, losing the cumulative effect of watching him manage a genuine security emergency with total competence. The missing wand-wave furnishing the hall is a small but characteristic expression of his effortless power.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 6 (Quidditch match / Harry falls) - Dumbledore's intervention
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scene 84-85: Hermione recounts that 'Dumbledore was really angry... I've never seen him like that before. He ran onto the field as you fell, waved his wand, and you sort of slowed down before you hit the ground. Then he whirled his wand at the dementors. Shot silver stuff at them. They left the stadium right away... He was furious they'd come onto the grounds.' The anger is described as unprecedented and directed at a genuine breach of his authority.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film Scene 6: The film shows Dumbledore as 'a tall figure' who 'raises an open hand to the heavens' and produces an explosion that slows Harry's fall and repels the dementors. While the action is present, his fury is not conveyed in the scene itself — the film cuts to the hospital wing where Hermione simply says 'Dumbledore was furious. After he saved you, he sent them straight off.' The unprecedented nature of his anger, and the physical description of him running onto the field, is reduced to a reported line.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book specifically flags that students have never seen Dumbledore that angry, which is itself characterisation — it shows that beneath his serene exterior there is a fierce protectiveness that can erupt when students are endangered. The film's version renders him as a competent magical intervention rather than a furious guardian. The distinction is small but contributes to a flatter emotional portrait.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 13 (Hospital wing / Time-Turner scene) - Dumbledore's aphoristic detachment
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scenes 209-217: Dumbledore enters the hospital wing, quickly asserts private authority by clearing the room, then speaks with precise, low urgency: 'It is your turn to listen, and I beg you will not interrupt me, because there is very little time.' He explains the legal and evidentiary problem with clinical clarity, explicitly tells Harry 'I do believe you' while explaining why he cannot act, and then gives the Time-Turner instruction with deliberate specificity ('Thirteenth window from the right of the West Tower'). His tone is grave and focused; he is solving a problem under pressure.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film Scene 13: Dumbledore enters, delivers a lyrical speech ('A child's voice, however honest and true, is meaningless to those who have forgotten how to listen'), gazes at a shooting star, and frames the Time-Turner hint as a series of poetic riddles about time being 'mysterious' and 'dangerous.' He hands out chocolate, offers the cryptic 'when in doubt, I find retracing my steps to be a wise place to begin,' and exits. The specific window location is replaced with 'topmost cell of the Dark Tower.'
damaging_scenes.explanation: This is the most damaging single scene in the corpus for Dumbledore's characterisation. The book's Dumbledore is urgently practical: he trusts Harry and Hermione with precise operational information because he respects their intelligence and the stakes are high. The film replaces this with an oracular, detached persona dispensing riddles and aphorisms while staring at stars. This shift — from a trusted adult giving children the tools and information they need, to a mystical figure speaking in fortune-cookie language — misrepresents his relationship with Harry. Book Dumbledore's trust is expressed through clarity and respect; film Dumbledore's is expressed through whimsy and deliberate obscurity. It also alters the relational dynamic: Harry in the book feels the weight of Dumbledore's direct guidance; in the film he is left to decode metaphors.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 16 (Buckbeak rescue, exterior) - Dumbledore's complicit amusement
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scene 239: When Buckbeak vanishes, Dumbledore says 'How extraordinary' with 'a note of amusement in his voice,' then redirects the executioner's attention: 'Search the skies, if you will... Hagrid, I could do with a cup of tea. Or a large brandy.' He is clearly aware something has happened and smoothly protects the situation.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film Scene 16: Dumbledore says 'How extraordinary!' with visible amusement, protects Hagrid by noting he was present the whole time, tells the Minister to 'search the skies,' and suggests a cup of tea or brandy. He also adds a line about 'Professor Dippet had those blackberries planted' to distract Fudge's attention from Buckbeak while Harry and Hermione lead him away.
damaging_scenes.explanation: This is largely faithful and the film actually adds the 'blackberries' distraction line which fits the character well. The damage here is minimal — the portrayal is consistent with the book. Scored low accordingly; included only because the corpus contains it as an explicit film beat to evaluate.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 18 (Clocktower corridor / return from time travel) - Dumbledore's reaction to success
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scenes 262-265: Dumbledore looks up as Harry and Hermione run toward him, and 'a wide smile appeared under the long silver mustache.' When Harry reports 'Sirius has gone, on Buckbeak,' Dumbledore 'beamed at them,' said 'Well done,' then listened carefully before confirming they had succeeded. His response is warm but swift and practical.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film Scene 18: Dumbledore stops at the door, looks up, and asks 'Well?' When Harry says 'He's free — Sirius. We… we did it,' Dumbledore asks 'Did what?' with a twinkle in his eye before swinging the door open. The 'Did what?' plays as a light joke or feigned innocence.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The 'Did what?' line, while charming, tips the characterisation slightly toward the arch-trickster persona rather than the book's quietly beaming pride. It is a minor drift but consistent with the film's broader pattern of making Dumbledore more enigmatically playful and less warmly direct. Low damage on its own but part of a cumulative tonal shift.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 19 (Lupin's departure) - Dumbledore's relationship with Lupin and the Firebolt reveal
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scenes 287-314: After Lupin's departure Dumbledore stays behind with Harry and has an extended, deeply personal conversation. He tells Harry he should be proud, explains why saving Pettigrew mattered ('It does not... You did a very noble thing'), reveals the magical bond created by saving a life, speaks gently about James Potter ('I knew your father very well'), and reflects on the Patronus: 'You know, Harry, in a way, you did see your father last night.... You found him inside yourself.' This scene establishes Dumbledore as Harry's most important adult confidant. Additionally, Book Scene 318-319 implies Dumbledore may have intervened with Snape's grading.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film Scene 19: Lupin departs after a brief exchange with Harry. There is no subsequent private scene between Dumbledore and Harry. The Firebolt arrives, apparently from Sirius (implied by the feather), skipping the book's ambiguity about Dumbledore possibly sending it (Book Scenes 119-121). The entire post-time-travel conversation in which Dumbledore gives Harry moral and emotional orientation is absent from the film corpus.
damaging_scenes.explanation: This is the second most structurally damaging absence in the corpus. The end-of-year conversation is where Dumbledore most fully inhabits his role as Harry's mentor, moral guide, and emotional anchor — roles that define their relationship across the entire saga. He explicitly validates Harry's actions, reframes the apparent failure as genuine heroism, introduces the concept of the life-debt (which pays off in Book 4), and connects Harry to his father in a way that gives the Patronus scene its full meaning. Without this scene, Dumbledore's mentorship function in this film is largely implied rather than demonstrated, and the Harry-Dumbledore relationship loses a defining moment of intimacy and guidance.

damaging_scenes.scene: Goblet of Fire - Harry's name from the Goblet / chamber confrontation
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Dumbledore asks 'Did you put your name into the Goblet of Fire, Harry?' calmly, and the narrative is explicit: he asked 'calmly.' He is described as looking at Harry with a searching, steady gaze. His demeanor throughout the chamber scene is measured and controlled, giving Harry the benefit of the doubt and firmly defending him to Karkaroff and Madame Maxime.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film has Dumbledore rush into the chamber in a visibly agitated state, grabbing Harry physically and shouting the question at him. The corpus shows Dumbledore saying 'Quiet! I can't think!' in an uncharacteristically flustered way, and then agreeing with Snape's 'let things unfold' position passively rather than defending Harry with the book's firm confidence.
damaging_scenes.explanation: One of the most iconic book characterization moments - Dumbledore's unshakeable calm and implicit trust in Harry - is reversed. The film Dumbledore appears to suspect Harry or at least lose composure, which undermines the established dynamic of Dumbledore as Harry's steady protector and the one adult who consistently believes him. This damages both character integrity and the Dumbledore-Harry relationship.

damaging_scenes.scene: Goblet of Fire - Dumbledore's response to Fudge regarding Barty Crouch Jr. / Voldemort's return
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Dumbledore delivers a lengthy, authoritative, and politically courageous confrontation with Fudge, laying out a specific action plan: remove the dementors, send envoys to the giants, recall the Order. He is described as radiating power, his eyes blazing, delivering the speech with controlled force. He explicitly tells Fudge they have reached 'a parting of the ways.'
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film reduces this to a much shorter exchange: 'A man has died here, Fudge. And he won't be the last. You must take action.' / 'Then for once show them some!' The detailed strategic vision, the moral authority, the specific prescriptions, and the parting-of-the-ways gravity are all absent. Fudge's dismissal of Barty Crouch Jr.'s testimony via dementor is present but Dumbledore's response is truncated.
damaging_scenes.explanation: This scene is a major arc moment: Dumbledore stepping forward as the leader of resistance against Voldemort and against Ministry denial. The book's version establishes his political courage, strategic foresight, and moral clarity. The film's truncation reduces him to a few blunt lines, losing the sense that he alone sees the full picture and is already mobilizing. This damages audience understanding of his role in the wider saga.

damaging_scenes.scene: Goblet of Fire - Dumbledore's Pensieve scene / conversation with Harry about his dreams
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Dumbledore uses the Pensieve scene to have a rich, private dialogue with Harry about Voldemort's return, the scar connection, the meaning of the dreams, Priori Incantatem, the Longbottoms, Snape's loyalty, and Bagman. He is reflective, wise, and candid about the limits of his own knowledge ('I have a theory, no more than that'). He gently redirects Harry's questions about Snape with firm but kind boundaries. The scene shows Dumbledore as someone carrying enormous weight but sharing it carefully with Harry.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film's Pensieve scene is heavily truncated. Dumbledore tells Harry 'I think it's unwise for you to linger over these dreams, Harry. I think it's best if you simply cast them away.' This is the opposite of the book's approach, where Dumbledore takes the dreams seriously as probable real events. The film Dumbledore dismisses Harry's visions rather than engaging with them as intelligence.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book Dumbledore treats Harry as a partner in understanding Voldemort's return, validating his experiences and sharing his own analysis. The film Dumbledore dismisses the dreams entirely, which misrepresents his character as incurious or evasive rather than deeply engaged. This also damages the mentor relationship and removes a key moment of Dumbledore's strategic intelligence being demonstrated.

damaging_scenes.scene: Goblet of Fire - Dumbledore mobilizing the resistance after Voldemort's return (hospital wing)
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: In the hospital wing, after Fudge leaves, Dumbledore orchestrates an immediate and detailed response: he activates Sirius, dispatches Snape back to the Death Eaters as a spy, tasks Bill Weasley with alerting Arthur, plans to contact Hagrid and Madame Maxime for a mission, and names the old crowd (Lupin, Arabella Figg, Mundungus Fletcher). He is shown as a general marshaling forces with calm authority and apprehension for Snape's safety.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: This entire mobilization sequence is absent from the film corpus. The film moves from the confrontation with Fudge directly to a brief scene with Harry in the dormitory. There is no activation of the resistance network, no dispatch of Snape, no naming of the Order members.
damaging_scenes.explanation: This is Dumbledore's primary structural function at the end of Goblet of Fire: transitioning from headmaster to general of the resistance. Its removal means the film audience has no sense of Dumbledore taking decisive action in response to Voldemort's return. His role as the organizing force against Voldemort - which is central to the saga's next three films - is not established. This is the single largest arc-level loss.

damaging_scenes.scene: Goblet of Fire - Dumbledore's speech at the Leaving Feast
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Dumbledore delivers a full, politically defiant speech at the Leaving Feast: he names Voldemort directly, explicitly states the Ministry does not want him to say this, honors Harry by name and raises a goblet to him, speaks to the international guests about unity, and closes with the 'remember Cedric' passage framed around the choice between what is right and what is easy. The speech is a public act of resistance and a moral statement.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film delivers an abbreviated version: Dumbledore names Voldemort as the killer, mentions the Ministry's objection to saying so, and gives a shorter unity speech. The explicit honoring of Harry by name with the raised goblet is absent from the film corpus. The 'what is right and what is easy' formulation appears but in the private dormitory scene rather than as a public declaration.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The public dimension of Dumbledore's courage - standing before the whole school and naming Voldemort against Ministry wishes - is reduced. The specific honoring of Harry publicly is lost. While the core content survives in abbreviated form, the full weight of the moment as a political act and a public rallying cry is diminished.

damaging_scenes.scene: Goblet of Fire - Dumbledore visiting Hagrid's hut after the Skeeter article
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The book has Dumbledore personally present in Hagrid's hut to support him through his crisis of confidence after the Rita Skeeter article. He makes gentle jokes about his own brother Aberforth, shows warmth and wit, refuses to accept Hagrid's resignation, and insists he return to work. This scene demonstrates Dumbledore's pastoral care, humor, loyalty to his staff, and his insistence on including marginalized people.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: This scene is entirely absent from the film corpus. There is no equivalent moment of Dumbledore supporting Hagrid through the fallout from the Skeeter article.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The scene is one of the warmest characterization moments for Dumbledore in the book, showing his humor, loyalty, and personal investment in those society marginalizes. Its absence contributes to a film Dumbledore who is primarily reactive and institutional rather than personally warm and proactively caring.

damaging_scenes.scene: Goblet of Fire - Dumbledore discovering the real Moody in the trunk / interrogating Barty Crouch Jr.
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Dumbledore takes complete command of the post-revelation scene: he sends McGonagall and Snape on specific tasks, personally opens each lock of the trunk, discovers Moody, administers Veritaserum, and conducts the full interrogation of Barty Crouch Jr. He is described as the only wizard Voldemort feared, radiating cold fury and terrible power. He then tells Harry 'he needs to understand' and insists Harry stay to hear everything.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film preserves the broad structure - Dumbledore bursts in, Veritaserum is administered, Crouch confesses - but compresses it significantly. The film corpus shows Dumbledore grabbing 'Moody' and slamming him against the wall physically, which is more viscerally aggressive than the book's cold, controlled fury. The detailed orchestration of sending people on tasks and the extended interrogation are compressed. The 'only wizard Voldemort feared' characterization beat is present implicitly.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The film's physical aggression (slamming against wall) substitutes for the book's more terrifying cold fury and methodical control. While the scene broadly works, the specific quality of Dumbledore's power - intellectual and commanding rather than physically reactive - is somewhat altered. The compression also loses the detailed orchestration that shows his mastery of the situation.

damaging_scenes.scene: Goblet of Fire - Dumbledore's private conversation with Harry after the graveyard (dormitory scene)
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Dumbledore insists Harry tell the full story immediately despite Sirius's protests, explaining 'Numbing the pain for a while will make it worse when you finally feel it.' He listens to every detail, asks clarifying questions, stands up sharply when Harry mentions Wormtail taking his blood, and shows a 'gleam of triumph' at the blood protection detail. He explains Priori Incantatem, discusses the echo-forms, and shows deep respect for Harry's courage.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film's equivalent scene is the dormitory conversation where Dumbledore says 'I never liked these curtains. Set them on fire in my fourth year. By accident, of course' and then discusses Priori Incantatem briefly before saying 'You have friends here. You're not alone.' The detailed debriefing, the blood-protection moment of near-triumph, and the extended Priori Incantatem explanation are condensed or absent.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book scene establishes that Dumbledore immediately prioritizes intelligence-gathering and Harry's psychological recovery through truth-telling. The film replaces much of this with a comfort-focused brief exchange that, while warm, loses Dumbledore's strategic engagement with what Harry witnessed, including the crucial blood-protection detail that has saga-level implications.

damaging_scenes.scene: Order of the Phoenix - Ministry hearing; Dumbledore arrives and departs without acknowledging Harry
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book establishes that Harry feels a powerful, fortifying emotion at seeing Dumbledore ('a fortified, hopeful feeling rather like that which phoenix song gave him') and desperately wants to catch Dumbledore's eye throughout the hearing. Dumbledore's deliberate avoidance is a conscious, painful choice driven by his fear of Voldemort exploiting their connection. After the acquittal, Dumbledore departs 'without looking once at Harry', and Harry later reflects with hurt that Dumbledore had visited Grimmauld Place without asking to see him. This behaviour is part of a sustained, explained pattern of protective distance.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film condenses the hearing to a brisk procedural scene (Film Scene 2-3). Dumbledore arrives, intercedes competently, and the moment of his ignoring Harry is not dramatised as a felt wound. There is no internal Harry reaction registering the hurt of being unseen, no 'without looking once at Harry' beat given weight. The film presents Dumbledore's competence without the accompanying emotional cost to Harry of being deliberately blanked by the one person he most wants to turn to.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book uses the hearing to establish both Dumbledore's brilliance and the painful asymmetry of his relationship with Harry at this point: Harry gains legal safety but loses emotional contact. The film captures the first without the second, flattening a key relationship beat that motivates Harry's growing resentment toward Dumbledore across the whole fifth year.

damaging_scenes.scene: Order of the Phoenix - Dumbledore's office post-battle; Harry wrecks the office (cut scene)
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The book devotes a long, climactic scene to Harry's grief-rage after Sirius's death: he destroys instruments in Dumbledore's office, screams, demands to be let out, and Dumbledore calmly absorbs it all without flinching, ultimately saying 'I daresay I have too many' possessions. This is the emotional climax of the book's Dumbledore arc — he accepts Harry's fury as deserved, takes full responsibility for Sirius's death, explains years of withholding, and weeps. It is the scene in which their relationship is fundamentally renegotiated.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: This scene is listed in the non-theatrical exclusions as cut from the theatrical release. The film replaces it with a brief exchange (Film Scene 10) in which Dumbledore says 'the fault is mine' and explains he distanced himself to protect Harry, and Harry says 'I care too much about you.' There is no destroyed office, no screaming, no prolonged confrontation, no Dumbledore absorbing Harry's physical rage, no extended confession of old-man mistakes, no prophecy explanation delivered in full dramatic context.
damaging_scenes.explanation: This is the single most damaging absence in the adaptation. The office-wrecking scene is the structural and emotional climax of Dumbledore's arc in Book 5: it is where he takes moral responsibility, explains his failures, reveals the prophecy, and demonstrates that he loves Harry enough to let Harry rage at him. Removing it means the audience never sees Dumbledore's full confession, never sees him weep, never experiences the cathartic renegotiation of the relationship. The replacement exchange is too short and too calm to carry this weight. The saga-level theme — that Dumbledore's greatest flaw is loving Harry so much he withheld truth — is severely compressed and loses most of its emotional power.

damaging_scenes.scene: Order of the Phoenix - Grimmauld Place kitchen; Dumbledore's absence from Harry's hearing night visit
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scene 141 establishes that Dumbledore visited Grimmauld Place the night before Harry's hearing and did not ask to see him. 'The thought that Dumbledore had been in the house on the eve of his hearing and not asked to see him made him feel, if it were possible, even worse.' This compounds Harry's sense of abandonment and feeds his growing resentment toward Dumbledore as a deliberate, ongoing pattern.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film does not include this beat. There is no moment where Harry learns Dumbledore was nearby and chose not to see him. The cumulative texture of Dumbledore's deliberate distancing — which in the book builds across multiple small moments — is largely absent.
damaging_scenes.explanation: While individually small, this beat contributes to the book's careful construction of Harry's alienation from Dumbledore. Its absence means the film's Harry has less justified grievance, weakening the emotional credibility of his resentment and making Dumbledore's later apology feel less earned.

damaging_scenes.scene: Order of the Phoenix - Dumbledore's Army confrontation in Dumbledore's office; Dumbledore takes blame
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scenes 609-652 show Dumbledore engineering an elaborate, witty escape from arrest while protecting Harry: he claims the DA was his idea, outmanoeuvres Fudge and two Aurors, and flees via Fawkes — all while giving Harry last urgent instructions about Occlumency. The scene showcases his strategic brilliance, courage, self-sacrifice, and dry humour ('I could break out, of course — but what a waste of time'). He also privately thanks Kingsley for the memory modification.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film Scene 5 includes this sequence and largely preserves it: Dumbledore takes responsibility, delivers the 'come quietly' line, and departs stylishly. The film does capture the essence of Dumbledore's agency and wit here. This is a relatively faithful moment.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The film mostly preserves this scene. Minor compression removes some of the book's extended wit (the 'waste of time breaking out' line, the private aside to McGonagall about Kingsley), slightly reducing the texture of Dumbledore's voice, but damage is minimal. Scored low accordingly.

damaging_scenes.scene: Order of the Phoenix - Ministry Atrium duel with Voldemort
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scenes 725-783 show Dumbledore duelling Voldemort with extraordinary controlled power and philosophical calm: he speaks about the nature of death and love mid-combat ('there are things much worse than death'), refuses to kill, and after Voldemort attempts to possess Harry, Dumbledore's response is to call 'Stay where you are, Harry!' with genuine fear in his voice — the only time he sounds frightened. He then calmly takes charge of the aftermath, issuing Fudge orders and arranging Harry's return.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film Scene 9 depicts the duel but compresses the philosophical dialogue significantly. The line 'It was foolish of you to come here tonight, Tom. The Orders are on their way' and Dumbledore's post-duel authority over Fudge are present. However, the extended philosophical exchange about death ('There is nothing worse than death, Dumbledore!' / 'You are quite wrong') is stripped to a minimal exchange. The nuanced portrait of Dumbledore as someone who fights without seeking to kill, and whose deepest weapon is understanding love and death better than Voldemort, is thinned.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The duel is the one moment in Book 5 where Dumbledore's philosophy becomes action. The dialogue mid-duel establishes the thematic core of the entire saga: Voldemort's inability to understand love is his fatal weakness. Stripping this reduces Dumbledore from a philosopher-warrior to a technically impressive duelist, weakening the saga-level thematic payoff.

damaging_scenes.scene: Order of the Phoenix - Throughout film; Dumbledore's deliberate avoidance of Harry presented without accumulated texture
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The book builds Dumbledore's avoidance of Harry across dozens of small moments: not looking at him at the hearing, not visiting him in Grimmauld Place, Snape being assigned Occlumency instead of Dumbledore himself, Harry noticing Dumbledore seems to look just over his shoulder rather than at him, etc. (Book Scenes 141, 193, 196, 272, 301, 411-417, 465-466, 492). This accumulation is essential: it makes Harry's resentment fully understandable and makes Dumbledore's later explanation and apology feel proportionate to a year of real abandonment.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film acknowledges the distance in dialogue (Film Scene 10: 'I thought by distancing myself from you... he'd be less tempted') but does not dramatise it through accumulated small moments. There is no scene where Harry registers the specific pain of being not-looked-at. The explanation is delivered but the behaviour it explains has not been sufficiently shown.
damaging_scenes.explanation: When the film's Dumbledore explains that he distanced himself all year, the audience has not felt that distance accumulate the way book readers have. The apology and explanation therefore land with less emotional weight. This undermines one of the book's central arcs: that Dumbledore's protective love manifested as a year of painful abandonment, and that this was a genuine mistake with genuine consequences.

damaging_scenes.scene: Order of the Phoenix - Post-battle Dumbledore's office (Film Scene 10, theatrical cut replacement)
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The book's extended office scene includes Dumbledore explicitly taking responsibility: 'It is my fault that Sirius died... almost entirely my fault.' He explains each decision error in detail — not teaching Occlumency himself, not telling Harry the prophecy sooner, allowing Snape's lessons to continue despite knowing the tension. He also reveals the prophecy in full, with the Pensieve, giving context to everything Harry has endured. Finally, he mentions he deliberately did not make Harry a prefect because he had 'enough responsibility to be going on with', and is seen with a tear on his face.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film Scene 10 (the replacement scene, which per the exclusion note is the post-Sirius office exchange that replaced the book's scene) gives Dumbledore: 'No, the fault is mine... I thought by distancing myself from you... I care too much about you.' Harry responds: 'Why didn't you tell me?' The prophecy is delivered not by Dumbledore in the office but as a discovered recording in the Department of Mysteries (Film Scene 7). The full moral accounting — Dumbledore cataloguing his specific failures — is gone.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The film's replacement condenses Dumbledore's confession to two sentences. The book's version is a sustained, unflinching self-examination by the most powerful wizard in the world, admitting that he let a boy suffer for years out of a misguided protective love. This is Dumbledore's defining moral moment in the entire series and the foundation for understanding his character in Books 6 and 7. The compression means the film Dumbledore never truly reckons with his failures at the granular level the books establish, reducing his characterisation from tragically flawed mentor to merely a kind old man who made one tactical error.

damaging_scenes.scene: Half-Blood Prince - Dumbledore arrives at Privet Drive / Dursley visit
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The book establishes a lengthy, characterful visit where Dumbledore commands the Dursleys with playful authority: conjuring mead that nudges them, finishing Vernon's sentences, making dry remarks about their rudeness, delivering a firm moral rebuke about Harry's treatment, and discussing Sirius's will, Kreacher, and Buckbeak. He is witty, warm, subtly threatening, and fully in control. This extended scene establishes Dumbledore's personality and his genuine care for Harry before their journey.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film entirely omits the Dursley visit and the formal collection of Harry from Privet Drive. Dumbledore instead appears on a London train platform, says only a few lines, and Apparates Harry directly to the Burrow. There is no Dursley confrontation, no mead, no moral rebuke, no Sirius's will discussion, no Kreacher resolution, and no private broom-shed conversation with Harry about Sirius's death, the prophecy, or the upcoming private lessons.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The Dursley visit is one of Dumbledore's richest characterisation scenes in the entire series: it shows his playful command, his moral authority, his dry wit, his genuine tenderness toward Harry, and his ability to be simultaneously disarming and formidable. Its total absence removes a defining portrait of who Dumbledore is outside Hogwarts, and strips Harry of the emotionally important private conversation in the broom shed about Sirius and the prophecy.

damaging_scenes.scene: Half-Blood Prince - Broom shed conversation (omitted)
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: After the Dursley visit, Dumbledore takes Harry aside in the Weasleys' broom shed and explicitly acknowledges Harry's grief over Sirius with compassion and specificity ('It was cruel that you and Sirius had such a short time together'). He praises Harry's resilience, advises him to share the prophecy with Ron and Hermione, announces the private lessons, and instructs Harry to keep his Invisibility Cloak at all times. This scene establishes Dumbledore's emotional attentiveness and the mentoring framework for the entire year.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The broom shed scene does not exist in the film. None of its content — the acknowledgement of Harry's grief, the praise, the instruction to share the prophecy, the announcement of lessons — is conveyed in any equivalent scene.
damaging_scenes.explanation: This is the scene that establishes the emotional core of the Dumbledore–Harry relationship for the sixth book: mutual trust, Dumbledore's attentiveness to Harry's inner life, and the framework of the private lessons as deliberate preparation. Its absence means the film's version of their mentoring relationship begins without this emotional foundation, weakening the resonance of Dumbledore's death.

damaging_scenes.scene: Half-Blood Prince - First private lesson (Pensieve session on Gaunt family / Bob Ogden memory)
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The book's first formal private lesson is a rich, extended Pensieve session covering the Gaunt family, Voldemort's heritage, Merope's love potion, and Tom Riddle Sr. Dumbledore contextualises everything carefully, makes observations about Voldemort's psychology, and creates a sustained pedagogical relationship with Harry. Multiple lessons follow, each adding layers.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film compresses the entire arc of Pensieve lessons drastically. The Gaunt family memory, Bob Ogden's visit, Morfin's memory, Hepzibah Smith's memory, and Dumbledore's own memory of the adult Voldemort requesting the teaching post are all absent. The film essentially shows only two Pensieve scenes: young Tom Riddle at the orphanage and the Slughorn Horcrux memory.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The private lessons are Dumbledore's primary narrative function in Half-Blood Prince: he is systematically equipping Harry with knowledge of Voldemort's past to enable the Horcrux hunt. Removing the majority of these lessons removes most of Dumbledore's active agency as a teacher and strategist, reducing him from a methodical architect of Harry's preparation to a character who mostly delivers exposition about Slughorn and then dies.

damaging_scenes.scene: Half-Blood Prince - Dumbledore's post-lesson discussions and explanations
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: After each Pensieve session, Dumbledore engages Harry in extended discussion: drawing attention to Riddle's trophy-collecting, his self-sufficiency, his contempt for the name Tom, his attachment to Hogwarts, his Horcrux theory, the significance of the diary, the ring, the locket, Hufflepuff's cup, Nagini, and the sixth unknown Horcrux. He also explicitly discusses his own fallibility and mistakes, and shares his reasoning about Voldemort's psychology at length. These conversations establish Dumbledore as a thinker and a humble, self-aware figure.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film's equivalent of this material is heavily compressed into a single post-Pensieve scene (scene 30 in the film corpus) where Dumbledore reacts to the Slughorn memory and briefly explains Horcruxes. The careful analytical discussions, the enumeration of likely Horcruxes, the discussion of the diary, the ring and how it was found, the humility about his own mistakes, and the extended conversation about love as Harry's power are all absent or drastically truncated.
damaging_scenes.explanation: Dumbledore's analytical, discursive voice — his habit of thinking aloud, making connections, acknowledging uncertainty, and treating Harry as an intellectual partner — is a defining character trait. The film reduces these exchanges to functional plot delivery, stripping Dumbledore of much of his distinctive intellectual personality.

damaging_scenes.scene: Half-Blood Prince - Dumbledore's 'haunted' reaction to the Slughorn memory (film scene 30)
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: In the book, after viewing the true Slughorn memory, Dumbledore is measured and analytical. He says 'I have been hoping for this piece of evidence for a very long time. It confirms the theory on which I have been working.' He proceeds to explain Horcrux theory carefully, discusses how many Horcruxes Voldemort likely made, and engages Harry as a thinking partner. He is calm, purposeful, and in command.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: In film scene 30, Dumbledore reacts to the memory with visible distress: 'This is beyond anything I imagined... I know now... you will see worse.' He appears shaken and emotionally destabilised, staring into the distance. This is a fundamentally different register — not the controlled, long-prepared strategist of the book, but a figure caught off-guard and overwhelmed.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book's Dumbledore has long suspected and prepared for this revelation; his reaction is that of a man whose theory is confirmed, not one who is shocked. The film's version makes him seem to have underestimated Voldemort, which undermines his characterisation as an omniscient and strategically far-sighted figure and misrepresents the emotional logic of the scene.

damaging_scenes.scene: Half-Blood Prince - Dumbledore's confrontation with Scrimgeour (Christmas at the Burrow)
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The book establishes through Harry's conversation with Scrimgeour that Dumbledore has actively intervened to protect Harry from Ministry pressure all year, and that he and Scrimgeour have a frosty, adversarial relationship over the Ministry's approach. Dumbledore is shown as a political operator who understands power and chooses his battles carefully. When Harry reports back 'Dumbledore's man through and through,' Dumbledore is visibly moved and responds with genuine warmth and dignity.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The Scrimgeour subplot is entirely absent from the film. There is no Ministry pressure on Harry, no Scrimgeour visit, and no moment where Harry declares himself Dumbledore's man and Dumbledore is moved by it.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The Scrimgeour scenes establish Dumbledore as a politically astute figure who shields Harry, and the 'Dumbledore's man through and through' exchange is a quietly important moment of mutual loyalty. Its absence loses a dimension of Dumbledore as a figure who operates strategically beyond Hogwarts walls.

damaging_scenes.scene: Half-Blood Prince - Snape/Dumbledore argument on Astronomy Tower (film scene 32)
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The book does not contain this scene. In the books, Hagrid overhears Dumbledore telling Snape he agreed to do something and Snape expressing reluctance — which Harry interprets as Dumbledore forcing Snape to investigate Malfoy. There is no direct confrontation depicted between them.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film scene 32 shows Harry eavesdropping on Snape telling Dumbledore he doesn't want to do 'this' anymore and asking if Dumbledore has considered that he takes too much for granted, with Dumbledore responding crisply that Snape agreed and there is nothing more to discuss. This is depicted as a tense power confrontation.
damaging_scenes.explanation: While this scene is drawn from a book reference (Hagrid's overheard conversation), dramatising it directly as an open confrontation changes the dynamic between Dumbledore and Snape. The book keeps their arrangement opaque and trusting; the film makes it appear as a coercive command relationship, which subtly alters how Dumbledore's trust in Snape reads and anticipates the Unbreakable Vow revelation in a way that is not present in the source.

damaging_scenes.scene: Half-Blood Prince - Astronomy Tower scene: Dumbledore immobilises Harry (omitted)
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: In the book, Dumbledore wordlessly immobilises Harry under the Invisibility Cloak before Malfoy arrives, making a deliberate choice to protect Harry at the cost of his own ability to defend himself. This act of self-sacrifice — Dumbledore's last active choice — is a profound moment that underlines his priorities. Harry understands immediately after Dumbledore's death that 'the second he had taken to perform the spell had cost him the chance of defending himself.'
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: In the film, Dumbledore instead verbally instructs Harry to hide below the tower through the lattice floor, and Harry obeys voluntarily. There is no wordless Body-Bind spell, no sacrifice of defensive capability, and no moment of Dumbledore actively choosing Harry's safety over his own survival.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The wordless immobilisation is Dumbledore's last major active choice in the narrative, and it is a crucial act of self-sacrifice that defines his character. By replacing it with a verbal instruction that Harry follows willingly, the film removes Dumbledore's agency in that final moment and loses the thematic resonance of him choosing Harry's life over his own defence. This is a significant structural loss.

damaging_scenes.scene: Half-Blood Prince - Astronomy Tower: Dumbledore's extended dialogue with Malfoy
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: In the book, Dumbledore engages Malfoy in a lengthy, patient, and strategically compassionate conversation: he identifies each of Malfoy's attempts on his life ('these are feeble attempts'), acknowledges that he has been protecting Malfoy all year by not confronting him, explains the situation to Malfoy ('I knew that you would have been murdered'), and explicitly offers him sanctuary for himself and his mother. He also draws Malfoy close to lowering his wand through a careful appeal to his humanity. The Death Eaters then arrive and Dumbledore continues to face them with composure.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film covers similar ground but compresses it considerably. Dumbledore still identifies the attempts and questions whether Malfoy's heart is in it. However, the extended sequence in which Dumbledore explicitly tells Malfoy he has been protecting him all year, explains his reasoning about not confronting him earlier, and offers specific sanctuary ('Come over to the right side, Draco... I can send members of the Order to your mother tonight') is significantly shortened. Key lines about Dumbledore's deliberate protection of Malfoy are absent.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book's Tower scene is Dumbledore's most explicit statement of his philosophy of mercy and his long-game strategy of protecting even those who threaten him. The compression loses some of the full articulation of why Dumbledore is the figure he is. The film retains enough to be broadly faithful but loses important nuance about his proactive protection of Malfoy.

damaging_scenes.scene: Half-Blood Prince - Cave scene: 'I am not worried, Harry. I am with you' (cut from theatrical release)
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: As Harry and Dumbledore swim out of the cave, Harry reassures a weakened Dumbledore that it will be all right. Dumbledore responds: 'I am not worried, Harry. I am with you.' This line is the emotional pinnacle of their relationship — Dumbledore expressing complete trust in Harry, reversing the usual dynamic of the powerful protecting the young.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Per the non-theatrical exclusions, the scene where Dumbledore says 'I am not worried, Harry. I am with you' on leaving the cave was cut from the theatrical release. The line does not appear in the film.
damaging_scenes.explanation: This line is one of the most important expressions of the Dumbledore–Harry relationship in the entire saga: it shows Dumbledore's trust in Harry as a person rather than merely a weapon or protégé, and it inverts the protective dynamic in a way that carries enormous emotional weight. Its loss is a meaningful reduction in the relationship's depth as portrayed on screen.

damaging_scenes.scene: Half-Blood Prince - Dumbledore's death and immediate aftermath: funeral
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The book includes Dumbledore's funeral as a rich, extended scene: merpeople singing, centaurs watching from the forest, Hagrid carrying the body, the white tomb forming from flames, Scrimgeour attempting to press Harry immediately after, and Harry's private grief and decision-making. The funeral establishes the full weight of Dumbledore's significance to the world and to Harry.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film omits Dumbledore's funeral entirely. After the wand-raising salute in the courtyard, the film cuts to the Astronomy Tower the following day with Harry, Hermione, Ron and Ginny discussing the fake Horcrux. There is no funeral scene, no white tomb, no gathering of the wizarding world, no Scrimgeour confrontation, and no formal farewell.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The funeral is the narrative seal on Dumbledore's arc and the moment that crystallises Harry's resolve and grief. Its absence means the film does not properly close Dumbledore's story or give the audience — or Harry — a formal moment of mourning. The emotional transition from his death to Harry's determination to continue the mission loses its structural anchor.

damaging_scenes.scene: Half-Blood Prince - Harry's confrontation with Dumbledore about Snape and Trelawney's revelation
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Harry discovers from Trelawney that it was Snape who overheard the prophecy and conveyed it to Voldemort. He races to Dumbledore in a fury, shouting accusations. Dumbledore listens and then delivers a careful, measured defence of Snape's remorse and his own reasons for trusting him, while acknowledging the gravity of Snape's original act. He also tells Harry they must go, choosing to take Harry even while Harry is in a rage. This exchange is important for establishing Dumbledore's unshakeable faith in Snape and his ability to hold complex moral positions.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The Trelawney revelation about Snape and the prophecy does not occur in the film. Harry does not confront Dumbledore about Snape before they leave for the cave. The entire dynamic of Dumbledore defending Snape while Harry rages is absent.
damaging_scenes.explanation: This confrontation is the last major conversation between Harry and Dumbledore and it establishes Dumbledore's unwavering trust in Snape as a conscious, informed choice rather than naivety. Its absence means the audience does not see Dumbledore make a clear-eyed defence of Snape in the moments before his death, which matters for understanding the full weight of 'Severus... please' on the tower and for the eventual revelation in Deathly Hallows.

damaging_scenes.scene: Half-Blood Prince - Dumbledore's office scene establishing private lesson framework and prophecy discussion
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The book's first formal private lesson includes Dumbledore explicitly telling Harry that he has decided to take a greater hand in his education, discussing the prophecy as the framework for everything, inviting Harry to share the prophecy content with Ron and Hermione, and explaining the lessons' purpose. He is forthcoming, treats Harry as a partner in a shared mission, and is explicitly humble about the limits of his own knowledge ('I may be as woefully wrong as Humphrey Belcher').
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film scene 18 (Dumbledore's office after the orphanage Pensieve) shows Dumbledore explaining that Slughorn possesses something he desires, that Harry should let Slughorn collect him, and that he will explain in time. The framework of the lessons is not explicitly established, the prophecy is not discussed, and Dumbledore's explicit invitation to Harry as a partner in reasoning is absent.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book carefully establishes that Dumbledore is treating Harry as a participant in a shared intellectual and strategic enterprise, not simply deploying him as a tool against Slughorn. The film version leaves the relationship more opaque and instrumental, reducing Harry to an asset Dumbledore is using to extract information rather than a student he is deliberately preparing.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 31 – Aberforth confrontation at the Hog's Head
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book establishes Aberforth's grievance as deeply personal and specific: Albus neglected Ariana while consumed by his friendship with Grindelwald and plans for wizard domination. Aberforth recounts in detail how Albus was 'always up in his bedroom reading his books and counting his prizes,' how Grindelwald used the Cruciatus Curse on Aberforth, how Albus failed to defend him, and how Ariana died in the ensuing fight. Harry internally resolves his doubts by deciding to trust the Dumbledore he knew, having already made peace with Dumbledore's flawed past during Dobby's burial. Harry's resolution is earned through sustained internal wrestling across many chapters.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Aberforth's accusation is reduced to a single vague line: 'My brother sacrificed many things in his journey to find power, including her. She was devoted to him — he gave her everything, but time.' No detail about Grindelwald's abuse, the duel, or the circumstances of Ariana's death is given. Harry's counter-resolution — 'I only care about the Dumbledore I knew. I trusted him' / 'I need to. Because if I don't, I don't know who I am anymore' — arrives almost immediately and without the weight of the book's prolonged crisis of faith. The emotional arc of Harry reconciling with Dumbledore's flawed legacy is collapsed into a brief exchange.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book spends dozens of pages having Harry genuinely doubt Dumbledore — his wisdom, his care, his honesty — before arriving at a hard-won trust. The film skips the substance of Aberforth's full testimony (no Grindelwald detail, no Cruciatus, no three-way duel, no ambiguity about who killed Ariana) and rushes Harry's reconciliation. This collapses a major arc beat: the audience never fully understands why Harry had reason to doubt, so his decision to trust feels like stubbornness rather than hard-won faith. Dumbledore's moral complexity is also significantly flattened.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 37 – Headmaster's office: Dumbledore instructs Snape to kill him
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book establishes Dumbledore's request as morally and psychologically layered. He acknowledges Snape's soul may be harmed, frames it as a favour to spare himself pain and to protect Draco, and engages Snape on whether it will harm his soul. The conversation also covers Dumbledore's broader plan for the Elder Wand — that he intended to die undefeated so the wand's power would be broken. Dumbledore's tone is measured, almost philosophical, and he shows genuine concern for Snape's moral integrity.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film's Dumbledore thunders: 'Too much! Nothing I could ask is too much. You know what is at stake! You more than anyone!' This outburst replaces the book's quiet, collaborative moral reasoning. The nuanced discussion about Snape's soul, Draco's soul, and Dumbledore's personal wish to avoid a painful death is absent. Dumbledore sounds coercive and self-righteous rather than wise and self-aware.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book's Dumbledore in this scene is characterised by calm acceptance of death and genuine solicitude for Snape's soul. The film replaces this with an uncharacteristic outburst that makes Dumbledore sound demanding and domineering.
